sequences.title: From $\dot x = Ax$ to the matrix exponential
sequences.summary: The solution of a linear system is a matrix exponential applied to the initial state, and the exponential of a matrix is defined by the same Taylor series as for a number.

initial.title: A linear system of ODEs
initial.explanation: The whole lecture is about this one equation: the rate of change of the state is a fixed matrix times the state. It is the cornerstone for everything later in the bootcamp.

steps.title: Sizes: a vector and a square matrix
steps.tex: \dot x = A x, \qquad x \in \mathbb{R}^n,\quad A \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}
steps.explanation: $x$ stacks $n$ state variables in a column. $A$ is $n \times n$: entry $a_{ij}$ says how much variable $j$ pushes on the rate of change of variable $i$.

steps.title: The solution: a matrix exponential
steps.explanation: The state at time $t$ is the matrix $e^{At}$ times the initial state $x(0)$. Order matters: a matrix acting on a column vector, so $e^{At}$ is on the left.

steps.title: Recall the scalar Taylor series
steps.explanation: For a number $a$ the exponential is an infinite sum of powers. Only products and sums appear, and those also make sense for square matrices.

steps.title: Plug in the matrix $At$
steps.explanation: Replace $a$ by $A$. The $1$ becomes the identity matrix $I$ and every term is an $n\times n$ matrix, so $e^{At}$ is an infinite sum of matrices. At $t = 0$ only $I$ survives, so $x(0) = I\,x(0)$ as it must.

steps.title: Not the exponential of each entry
steps.explanation: Powers $A^2, A^3, \dots$ mix the entries, so the matrix exponential is not computed entry by entry (an off-diagonal $0$ in $A$ would wrongly give $e^0 = 1$). Summing the series by hand is impractical for a $5 \times 5$ matrix, which motivates the eigenvector route.

sequences.title: Eigenvectors, eigenvalues and $AT = TD$
sequences.summary: Eigenvectors are the directions that $A$ only stretches. Collecting them as the columns of $T$ and the eigenvalues on the diagonal of $D$ gives $AT = TD$.

initial.title: The eigenvalue equation
initial.explanation: A nonzero vector $c$ is an eigenvector of $A$ if multiplying by $A$ only rescales it by the number $\lambda$, its eigenvalue.

steps.title: Most vectors turn, eigenvectors do not
steps.explanation: For this example matrix a generic vector $v$ comes out pointing in a new direction. $c_1 = (1, 0)$ and $c_2 = (1, 1)$ stay on their own lines; a negative $\lambda$ flips them to the opposite side and rescales.

steps.title: Collect eigenvectors and eigenvalues
steps.explanation: $T$ has the eigenvectors as columns. $D$ is diagonal with the matching eigenvalues in the same order and zeros everywhere else.

steps.title: $A$ acts on each column of $T$
steps.tex: AT = \begin{bmatrix} Ac_1 & Ac_2 & \cdots & Ac_n \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \lambda_1 c_1 & \lambda_2 c_2 & \cdots & \lambda_n c_n \end{bmatrix}
steps.explanation: A matrix times $T$ multiplies each column of $T$ separately. Each column is an eigenvector, so column $i$ becomes $\lambda_i c_i$.

steps.title: Right-multiplying by $D$ scales columns
steps.tex: TD = \begin{bmatrix} \lambda_1 c_1 & \lambda_2 c_2 & \cdots & \lambda_n c_n \end{bmatrix} \;\Rightarrow\; AT = TD
steps.explanation: Multiplying $T$ on the right by a diagonal matrix scales column $i$ by $\lambda_i$. That is exactly the previous result, so $AT = TD$. Note the order: $DT$ would scale rows instead.

steps.title: When does this work?
steps.explanation: Distinct eigenvalues are enough but not required: $A = 2I$ has a repeated eigenvalue and is still diagonal. A defective matrix such as $\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{bmatrix}$ has only one eigenvector direction; it needs generalized eigenvectors and a Jordan form, which the lecture only mentions.

sequences.title: Eigenvector coordinates: $x = Tz$ gives $\dot z = Dz$
sequences.summary: Describe the state by how much of each eigenvector it contains. In those coordinates the dynamics matrix becomes the diagonal $D$.

initial.title: A change of coordinates
initial.explanation: $z$ lists how much of each eigenvector (each column of $T$) is needed to build $x$. With the example $T$, the point $x = (2, 1)$ is $1\cdot c_1 + 1\cdot c_2$.

steps.title: New axes along the eigenvectors
steps.explanation: The grid of $z$ coordinates is the standard grid sheared by $T$: its lines run along $c_1$ and $c_2$. The axes are not perpendicular, which is fine as long as they are independent.

steps.title: Going back: $z = T^{-1}x$
steps.explanation: Independent eigenvectors make $T$ invertible. Use the inverse, not the transpose: they agree only when the eigenvectors are orthonormal, which this example's are not.

steps.title: Differentiate: $T$ is constant
steps.explanation: $T$ does not change with time, so the derivative passes straight through it.

steps.title: Substitute into $\dot x = Ax$
steps.tex: T\dot z = A x = A T z
steps.explanation: Replace $\dot x$ by $T\dot z$ on the left and $x$ by $Tz$ on the right. $T$ stays to the right of $A$.

steps.title: Multiply by $T^{-1}$ on the left
steps.explanation: Multiply both sides on the left by $T^{-1}$; on the left side $T^{-1}T = I$. Multiplying on the right instead would not make sense for the vector $\dot z$.

steps.title: The dynamics are diagonal
steps.explanation: From $AT = TD$, multiplying on the left by $T^{-1}$ gives $T^{-1}AT = D$. In eigenvector coordinates the system is $\dot z = Dz$: the boxed result of the lecture.

sequences.title: Decoupled modes and $e^{Dt}$
sequences.summary: A diagonal system splits into $n$ separate scalar equations, each solved by one exponential. Stacked, they form $e^{Dt}$.

initial.title: The diagonal system
initial.explanation: This is the equation from the previous section. Writing it out shows why diagonal is so convenient.

steps.title: Write it out
steps.tex: \frac{d}{dt}\begin{bmatrix} z_1 \\ z_2 \\ \vdots \\ z_n \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \lambda_1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \lambda_2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \ddots & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & \lambda_n \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} z_1 \\ z_2 \\ \vdots \\ z_n \end{bmatrix}
steps.explanation: All off-diagonal entries of $D$ are zero. Read row by row: row $i$ of $D$ has one nonzero entry, $\lambda_i$, in column $i$.

steps.title: Each row involves one variable
steps.tex: \dot z_1 = \lambda_1 z_1,\quad \dot z_2 = \lambda_2 z_2,\quad \ldots,\quad \dot z_n = \lambda_n z_n
steps.explanation: The equations are decoupled: $\dot z_1$ depends only on $z_1$, $\dot z_2$ only on $z_2$, and so on. Each mode evolves independently of the others.

steps.title: Solve each scalar equation
steps.explanation: Each line is the scalar equation $\dot y = \lambda y$, solved by an exponential times its own initial value.

steps.title: Stack them: $e^{Dt}$
steps.tex: z(t) = e^{Dt} z(0), \qquad e^{Dt} = \begin{bmatrix} e^{\lambda_1 t} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \ddots & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & e^{\lambda_n t} \end{bmatrix}
steps.explanation: Exponentials on the diagonal and zeros off it (the off-diagonal entries are $0$, not $e^0 = 1$). For diagonal $D$ every power $D^k$ is diagonal with entries $\lambda_i^k$, so the series gives exactly this. The book writes $\Lambda$ for the lecture's $D$.

steps.title: Each mode on its own clock
steps.explanation: In the guide's example ($\lambda_1 = -1$, $\lambda_2 = -2$) both modes decay, the second twice as fast. Changing $z_1(0)$ would not affect $z_2$ at all.

sequences.title: Why $e^{At} = T e^{Dt} T^{-1}$
sequences.summary: Rewrite $A$ as $TDT^{-1}$, watch the inner $T^{-1}T$ pairs cancel in every power, and factor $T$ and $T^{-1}$ out of the series.

initial.title: Start from the series
initial.explanation: We want a formula for $e^{At}$ that only needs $e^{Dt}$, which is easy. The tool is the eigen relation $AT = TD$.

steps.title: Solve $AT = TD$ for $A$
steps.tex: AT = TD \;\Rightarrow\; A = T D T^{-1}
steps.explanation: Multiply both sides on the right by $T^{-1}$: $ATT^{-1} = A$. The $T^{-1}$ must go on the right, because that is where $T$ sits next to $A$.

steps.title: Square it and cancel the middle
steps.explanation: Matrix products are associative, so the adjacent pair $T^{-1}T$ in the middle can be grouped and equals $I$. Only that adjacent pair cancels; the outer $T$ and $T^{-1}$ stay.

steps.title: Every power works the same way
steps.explanation: In $(TDT^{-1})(TDT^{-1})\cdots(TDT^{-1})$ each inner $T^{-1}T$ cancels, leaving $k$ copies of $D$ between one $T$ and one $T^{-1}$.

steps.title: Substitute into the series
steps.explanation: Replace each $A^k$ by $TD^kT^{-1}$, and write the identity as $I = TT^{-1}$ so that the first term has the same shape as the others.

steps.title: Factor $T$ left and $T^{-1}$ right
steps.explanation: Every term has $T$ on the far left and $T^{-1}$ on the far right; the powers of $t$ and the factorials are scalars and can sit anywhere. Factor $T$ out to the left and $T^{-1}$ to the right, keeping the order.

steps.title: Recognize $e^{Dt}$
steps.explanation: The bracket is the series of $e^{Dt}$, the easy diagonal exponential. So the hard exponential $e^{At}$ costs one diagonal exponential and two matrix products.

sequences.title: Map, evolve, map back (the linked 22:22 moment)
sequences.summary: Read $x(t) = Te^{Dt}T^{-1}x(0)$ from right to left: into eigenvector coordinates, forward in time there, back to physical coordinates. Worked with numbers.

initial.title: The solution in physical coordinates
initial.explanation: Combine $x(t) = e^{At}x(0)$ with $e^{At} = Te^{Dt}T^{-1}$. Read it from right to left, the order in which the matrices act on $x(0)$.

steps.title: Three stages
steps.explanation: $T^{-1}x(0) = z(0)$ maps the start into eigenvector coordinates, $e^{Dt}$ advances it there (decoupled and easy), and $T$ maps the result back. This is the interpretation at 22:22 in the lecture.

steps.title: Map: $z(0) = T^{-1}x(0)$
steps.explanation: Guide's example: $T = \begin{bmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{bmatrix}$, $D = \mathrm{diag}(-1, -2)$, $A = TDT^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix}-1&-1\\0&-2\end{bmatrix}$, $x(0) = (2, 1)$. Then $z(0) = (2 - 1,\ 1) = (1, 1)$. (The transpose would give $(2, 3)$, which is wrong.)

steps.title: Evolve: $z(t) = e^{Dt}z(0)$
steps.explanation: Each eigen-coordinate decays on its own. At $t = \ln 2$, $e^{-t} = 1/2$ and $e^{-2t} = 1/4$.

steps.title: Map back: $x(t) = Tz(t)$
steps.tex: x(t) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} e^{-t} \\ e^{-2t} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} e^{-t} + e^{-2t} \\ e^{-2t} \end{bmatrix} \overset{t=\ln 2}{=} \begin{bmatrix} 3/4 \\ 1/4 \end{bmatrix}
steps.explanation: Multiply by $T$: $x_1 = z_1 + z_2$ and $x_2 = z_2$. In physical coordinates the two exponentials are mixed, which is why $A$ is not diagonal.

steps.title: Check against $\dot x = Ax$
steps.explanation: Differentiate the formula at $t = 0$: $(-e^{-t} - 2e^{-2t},\ -2e^{-2t}) \to (-3, -2)$. The right-hand side $Ax(0)$ gives the same vector, and $x(0) = (1 + 1, 1) = (2, 1)$ matches too.

steps.title: Recap and what comes next
steps.explanation: Think in eigenvector coordinates, where the modes are decoupled; map back when you need physical values. The lecture closes by deferring stability, discrete time and control inputs $+Bu$ to the next videos.
